chunks: 34 - Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Bashir from Ibn Abi Ghufilet al-Hasan ibn Ayyub from Dawud ibn Kathir al-Raqqi from Bashr ibn Abi Ghaylan al-Shaybani said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the slaughtered meat of the Jews, Christians, and Al-Nussab (those who reject the Imams), so he turned his cheek and said, 'Eat it until a certain day.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Those who oppose the Family of Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) are of two types: a type whose slaughtered meat is permissible to eat, and they are those who do not oppose the Family of Muhammad and show their love for them; and the second type whose slaughtered meat is not permissible, and they are the Khawarij and those who oppose them from among the haters of the Family of Muhammad (peace be upon them).

35 - That which indicates the first type is what was narrated - Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan ibn Yusuf ibn Aqil from Muhammad ibn Qays from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'The slaughtered meat of whoever follows the word of Islam, fasts, and prays for you is permissible if the name of Allah is mentioned upon it.'

key_terms.إِلَى يَوْمٍ مَا: Until a certain day (indicating temporary permissibility or uncertainty)
key_terms.الْخَوَارِج: The Khawarij (a sect known for opposing the Ahl al-Bayt)
key_terms.ضَارَعَهُمْ: Opposed them / were contrary to them
key_terms.فَلَوَى شِدْقَهُ: He turned his cheek (a gesture of hesitation or ambiguity)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating the meat of Jews, Christians, and Al-Nussab according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) provides a nuanced ruling by distinguishing between general monotheists and those specifically hostile to the Ahl al-Bayt, categorizing the latter (like the Khawarij) as having impermissible meat. This view is supported by the tradition of Imam al-Baqir (AS) citing Imam Ali (AS), which establishes that the key criterion for permissibility is the public profession of Islam and the performance of prayer, provided Allah's name is invoked. This highlights the Shia emphasis on theological alignment with the Ahl al-Bayt alongside ritual correctness in dietary laws.
